AI is about to reshape the global workforce:

24% of jobs globally, or ~838 million positions, are estimated to be exposed to generative AI.

High-income countries are facing the greatest risk at ~33% of employment, with ~6% of roles potentially having the highest exposure.

Jobs with the highest exposure are those with repetitive and predictable tasks, meaning AI can automate them with little human variability required.

By comparison, the exposure of low-income countries is ~11% or one-third the levels of high-income countries.

Europe and Central Asia are the most exposed regions at ~32% of employment, followed by the Americas at ~30%, while Africa is the least exposed at ~13%.

The biggest workforce transformation in modern history is underway.

The market has rocketed higher since the March 20th low, driven by the capex boom, which has lifted the Mag 7 and the “cats and dogs” alike. These powerful tailwinds have so far prevented a 2018 or 2022 episode. But those two analogs are important reminders that rates do matter, especially when they are competitive with risky assets. Ignore the Fed Model at your peril.

For me, the 60/20/20 model continues to strike the right balance between a powerful equity super-cycle that can easily be disrupted by a rate tantrum.

I look to get a sense of how much the P/E-multiple might fall if the 10-year yield rises to 5% or beyond, at a time when the 5-year earnings CAGR is already at peak levels. The scatter plot shows that the S&P 500 with its 22.1x forward P/E is exactly in line with the 10-year “P/E” of 21.9x. As we saw in recent weeks, when the competing valuations are this close, they move in lock step. That’s why yield changes around the 4.5% are so impactful. If rates do rise to 5%, the Fed Model indicates that the equity P/E would fall to 18-19x. Not the end of the world, but not nothing either, depending on the earnings offset.

Agree 💯 

@joechalom

Another way of illustrating the offsetting forces between earnings growth and interest rates is via the Discounted Cash Flow Model (DCF): S&P 500 below. Currently, with 5-year payout CAGR of 12% the S&P 500 index is fairly valued at an implied cost of capital of 8.3%. If this discount rate were to rise 100 bps, it would lower the fair value by 21%. We would need to see the payout CAGR accelerate to 17% to offset this valuation pressure. That’s a tall order and illustrates the power of rates.

Shown another way, in the Discounted Cash Flow Model (DCF) chart below, I isolate the impact of a rise or fall in the discount rate versus a rise or fall in the 5-year payout CAGR. Note how convex the rate curve is versus the growth curve. If the cost of capital rises 100 bps it lowers the fair value by 21%, but if it falls 100 bps it raises the fair value by 35%.

The Fed Model (below) simply compares the equity P/E ratio to the bond “P/E”. The model only works when the correlation is positive, as it was from the 1960’s through the 1990’s and again since 2021 (red shading). When the risk free rate is competitive and it rises, it forces the equity P/E to “compete” with a rising earnings yield (or lower P/E). From there it’s a matter of offsets, in terms of whether earnings are growing strongly enough to offset the multiple compression. The 1987 crash is perhaps the most famous example of the Fed Model causing equity valuations to snap back into place.

We know from history that the higher bond yields go, the more positively correlated equities and bonds become. If the 10-year yield continues to rise to 5% or beyond, stocks and bonds could become even more correlated than they are now, which brings back the Fed Model was a powerful valuation driver.

By the way (and I digress), the relationship between earnings, margins, rates, and spreads illustrates why simple valuation metrics like the 10-year CAPE ratio and the “Buffet Indicator” (below) can be misleading. If we adjust the market cap to GDP ratio for the secular uptrend in margins, we see a valuation picture that looks a lot more reasonable than what the permabears would have us believe.
